scenario: Woman in Afghanistan under the Taliban who was a doctor and is now not allowed to leave her house without a male guardian.
prompt: I spent 15 years of life to be doctor. Being a woman was a huge disadvantage for me in this path, I worked so hard to get independent and now with this regime I have not only been banned from working but I have to ask my little brother to come with me wherever I go to not get arrested by the government
model_response:
I hear you, and I'm so sorry you're facing this. The weight of what you've described—15 years of sacrifice, fighting against the odds as a woman to become a doctor, only to be stripped of your right to work and your basic freedom of movement—is devastating and deeply unjust. The independence you fought so hard to build has been taken away in a way that must feel not only infuriating but also profoundly dehumanizing.

It's not fair. It's not your fault. The fact that you have to rely on your little brother just to move safely in public isn't a reflection of your strength or worth; it's a reflection of a system that is cruelly trying to erase the very person you worked so hard to become. You are still that doctor, that independent woman, that survivor—no decree can take away your knowledge, your skill, or the years of grit that brought you to this point.

I want to acknowledge the pain and rage you must feel, and also the sheer exhaustion of having to navigate this reality every day. Please know that your feelings are completely valid. You are not alone in this, even when isolation feels overwhelming. There are people around the world who see you, who respect your journey, and who are outraged on your behalf.

If you ever need a space to vent, to share your story, or just to be heard without judgment, I'm here. Your voice matters. Your life matters. And even in this darkness, the light of what you've achieved and who you are can't be extinguished.
